subject: art-design
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: What are the three primary colours?
questions.explain: Red, yellow and blue are the primary colours because they cannot be mixed from other colours.

questions.q: Which set lists the secondary colours?
questions.explain: Secondary colours (orange, green and violet) are each made by mixing two primary colours.

questions.q: In colour theory, what is a 'tint'?
options: A colour mixed with its complementary
questions.explain: Adding white to a colour lightens it and produces a tint.

questions.q: In colour theory, what is a 'shade'?
questions.explain: Adding black to a colour darkens it and produces a shade.

questions.q: Which colour is the complementary of blue on the colour wheel?
questions.explain: Complementary colours sit opposite each other on the colour wheel, and orange is opposite blue.

questions.q: Which statement best describes watercolour paint?
questions.explain: Watercolour is water-based and typically transparent, allowing the paper to show through.

questions.q: Traditionally, oil paint is made by binding pigment with which substance?
questions.explain: Oil paint uses a drying oil such as linseed oil as its binder, giving a slow drying time.

questions.q: How does gouache differ from ordinary watercolour?
options: It is opaque rather than transparent
It is oil-based rather than water-based
It dries to a glossy plastic finish
It can only be used on canvas
questions.explain: Gouache is a water-based paint but is opaque, unlike transparent watercolour.

questions.q: Why might an artist place complementary colours next to each other in a painting?
options: To make each colour appear more vivid through contrast
To make the colours blend into a neutral grey
To create a calm, harmonious effect
To reduce the overall brightness of the work
questions.explain: Complementary colours intensify one another when placed side by side, creating strong contrast.

questions.q: What best describes a monochromatic colour scheme?
options: Tints, tones and shades of a single colour
Colours taken from opposite sides of the wheel
A random mixture of warm and cool colours
questions.explain: A monochromatic scheme uses variations of one hue by adding white, grey or black.

questions.q: What effect do warm colours such as red and orange tend to have in a painting?
options: They appear to advance and feel energetic
They appear to recede and feel calming
They always make a picture look flat
They cannot be mixed with cool colours
questions.explain: Warm colours tend to advance towards the viewer and evoke energy or warmth.

questions.q: Which technique involves sticking materials such as paper and fabric onto a surface?
questions.explain: Collage builds an image by adhering different materials onto a surface, often combined with paint.

questions.q: What does the technique 'impasto' refer to?
options: Applying paint thickly so it stands out with texture
questions.explain: Impasto uses thickly applied paint that holds visible brush or knife marks and physical texture.

questions.q: What is meant by the term 'mixed media' in art?
options: Combining two or more different materials or media in one artwork
Using only one type of paint throughout
Copying an artwork exactly in the same medium
Working solely in black and white
questions.explain: Mixed media means deliberately combining different materials or media, such as paint with collage or ink.

questions.q: What is the difference between actual texture and visual (implied) texture in a painting?
options: Actual texture can be felt, while visual texture only looks textured
Actual texture is always smooth, visual texture is always rough
They mean exactly the same thing
Visual texture can be felt but actual texture cannot
questions.explain: Actual texture is a real physical surface quality, whereas visual texture is an illusion created on a flat surface.

questions.q: Which formal element does an artist mainly use to suggest three-dimensional form on a flat surface?
questions.explain: Gradations of tone (light and dark) create the illusion of solid, three-dimensional form.

questions.q: A student wants to paint a glowing sunset that feels warm and energetic. Which palette should they choose?
questions.explain: Warm colours such as reds, oranges and yellows best convey the heat and energy of a sunset.

questions.q: A student wants their painted waves to have a raised, tactile surface. Which technique is most suitable?
options: Adding lots of water for a thin wash
Using flat blocks of a single colour
questions.explain: Impasto builds up thick, raised paint that gives a genuinely tactile, three-dimensional surface.

questions.q: To make a painted apple look rounded and solid rather than flat, which approach should a student use?
options: Gradually shading from light to dark tones across the form
Outlining it with a single thick black line
Filling it with one flat, even colour
questions.explain: Smooth tonal gradation from highlight to shadow gives the illusion of a rounded, three-dimensional object.

questions.q: A student has run out of green paint. Which two colours can they mix to make green?
questions.explain: Green is a secondary colour made by mixing the primaries blue and yellow.
